extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO (patent agents, trademark correspondents), trademark and patent attorneys, and participants in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and rules governing who may sign and file trademark documents via TEAS, limits on domestic representatives/correspondents, prohibited conduct (e.g., forging signatures, aiding unauthorized practice), and the USPTO disciplinary criteria and sanctioning factors applied when practitioners violate those rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documents must be signed by a proper person
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents filed in connection with a trademark application or registration must be signed by a proper person. 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(e); TMEP § 611.02.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: trademark documents that require a verification of the facts, such as an initial application or Statement of Use, must be sworn to in a declaration signed by the owner or the owner's authorized representative. A person who does not satisfy one of the acceptable categories cannot sign on behalf of an owner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who qualifies as an authorized signatory
rubrics_metrics.description: A person properly authorized to sign a declaration on behalf of an owner is either (i) a person with legal authority to bind the owner (e.g., a corporate officer or general partner); (ii) a person with firsthand knowledge of the facts and actual or implied authority to act on behalf of the owner; or (iii) an attorney with a power of attorney from the owner. 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(e)(1); TMEP § 611.03(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If none of these three requirements is satisfied, the person cannot sign a trademark document on behalf of an owner. When a document must be signed by someone with legal authority to bind a corporation, 'a corporate officer must sign.' TMEP § 611.06(d). Usual officer titles include President, Vice-President, Secretary, Treasurer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response to Office Action signature requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A Response to Office Action must be signed consistent with procedures in 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(e)(2), see 37 C.F.R. § 2.62(b), TMEP § 712: signed by the owner, a qualified practitioner, or someone with legal authority to bind the owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses and filings that could effectuate a change in an applicant's rights require signatories with broad authority (not just authority over trademark rights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited role of domestic representative and correspondent
rubrics_metrics.description: The procedures for trademark application proceedings allow a limited, non-signatory role for a 'domestic representative' and a 'correspondent.' A domestic representative is appointed by a foreign applicant to receive notices; a correspondent is a designated address for USPTO correspondence. TMEP §§ 609-610; TMEP §§ 609.04, 611.06(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither domestic representatives nor correspondents may prosecute an application or represent a party before the USPTO unless they are (a) a qualified practitioner recognized by the USPTO as the representative of the applicant/registrant, or (b) someone with legal authority to bind a juristic applicant (i.e., a corporate officer). Acting beyond these limits constitutes practice before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: TEAS signature methods and their legal effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Three acceptable signature methods available when filing through TEAS: Direct, Esign-on (E-mail Text Form to second party), and Hsign-on (handwritten pen-and-ink signature). TMEP § 611.01(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct: appropriate signatory personally enters name between slashes (e.g., /Name/); default method; saved forms lose signature and require reentry at filing to ensure personal verification at time of filing. XML shows <esignature-type> DIRECT. Esign-on: document emailed within TEAS to a signatory who signs and the form is returned; XML shows ESIGN-ON. Hsign-on: print, obtain handwritten signature, scan and attach (PDF/JPEG); XML shows HSIGN-ON. Choosing a method has procedural and evidentiary implications (e.g., whether signature was personally entered at filing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on signing another person's name electronically
rubrics_metrics.description: A person may not electronically sign another person's name to a trademark document and file that document with the Office. TMEP § 611.01(b) and (c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entering another person's electronic signature in the Direct or other TEAS methods (e.g., entering '/SomeoneElse/' yourself) is improper and violates the signature rules. Attaching a scanned handwritten signature and simultaneously entering an electronic signature for that person, without their personal act at filing, is inconsistent with signature method rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: TEAS help and responsibility to learn signature rules
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a hyperlink in TEAS forms to a Help screen providing additional information about who is a proper signatory for each type of form. USPTO rules govern who may sign forms in trademark proceedings. TMEP § 611.01(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners are expected to educate themselves about these rules; failure to do so cannot be relied upon as a defense. The Direct method's reentry requirement is purposeful to ensure verification of facts by the signer at time of filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO will not proactively investigate authorizations if signature appears proper
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO does not proactively investigate filings that appear correct on their face to determine if a signatory is authorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a signature appears proper on its face, USPTO staff may not question authorization, which creates an incentive for correct compliance with signature and signatory rules. Concealment (using another's signature and listing your own contact) can delay discovery of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign attorneys may not practice before the USPTO in trademark matters
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.1, 11.14(a) and (c), and TMEP § 602.03 prohibit foreign attorneys from practicing before the Office in trademark matters unless authorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign attorneys preparing trademark filings for U.S. trademark prosecution must comply with limitations; assisting or allowing foreign attorneys to practice in prohibited ways can constitute unauthorized practice and lead to discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aiding unauthorized practice is prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct to aid others in the unauthorized practice of law before the USPTO. 37 C.F.R. § 11.505.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepting filings prepared by foreign attorneys and filing them when those foreign attorneys are not authorized to practice before the Office can constitute aiding unauthorized practice. Paying, assisting, or otherwise facilitating such filings may trigger disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to 'engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.' 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5); 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include filing documents with forged signatures, assisting unauthorized practice, and knowingly violating exclusion orders; such conduct undermines public confidence and the efficiency of the trademark registration process. Case law cited: United States v. Johnson; In re Vohra; Liles; In re Kroll.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of specific disciplinary rules implicated by misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The ALJ found violations of multiple USPTO disciplinary rules, including 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a) (disreputable misconduct); § 10.23(b)(4) (deceit and misrepresentations to the USPTO); § 11.804(c) (deceit and misrepresentations to the USPTO); § 11.303(a)(1) (failure to correct misrepresentations made to the Office); § 10.77(a) (handling matters she was not competent to handle); § 11.505 (aiding others in the unauthorized practice of law); and § 10.23(b)(5) and § 11.804(d) (conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions encompass dishonesty, deceit, incompetence, failure to correct false statements, aiding unauthorized practice, and conduct that prejudices the administration of justice. Violation of one or more can support disciplinary sanctions including exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors for exclusion (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: An ALJ imposing exclusion must explain the reason after considering four factors: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty to a client, public, legal system, or profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) existence of aggravating or mitigating factors. 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)(1)-(4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application: the ALJ found duty violations (competence and integrity), intentional/knowing misconduct, potential for significant injury (even absent proven actual injury), and aggravating factors (dishonest motive, pattern over time, refusal to acknowledge misconduct). Prior clean disciplinary record is a mitigating factor. The combination of these informs whether exclusion is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof for affirmative defenses in disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellant must prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence. 37 C.F.R. § 11.49.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing requires evidence producing a firm belief or conviction of the truth of the allegations. Failure to satisfy this burden results in rejection of affirmative defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process expectations in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Due process in disciplinary proceedings requires reasonable notice of charges and meaningful opportunity to be heard (ability to present evidence, cross-examine witnesses, and argue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participation in pre-hearing procedures, hearings, and opportunity to present testimony and witnesses satisfies due process; claiming lack of earlier notice of wrongdoing is insufficient where resources (TMEP, TEAS Help) and opportunity to learn rules existed and the practitioner participated fully in the proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation of competence and to learn procedural rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are charged with educating themselves as to the rules governing proper signatures and filing of documents with the USPTO; failure to do so is a breach of duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ALJ noted Appellant failed to learn TEAS rules and TMEP requirements. Competence includes understanding who may sign, how TEAS methods operate, and limitations on domestic representative roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and post-discipline obligations (orders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedial and administrative orders may include: public notice of discipline (37 C.F.R. § 11.59), dissociation of the practitioner's name from Customer Numbers and PKI certificates, prohibition from obtaining or applying for a Customer Number until reinstated, and compliance with duties of disciplined practitioners (37 C.F.R. § 11.58).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discipline can include exclusion from practice before the Office in patent, trademark, and other non-patent matters; obligations to notify and administrative restrictions on access to USPTO filing resources are enforced as part of the sanction.
